nature-mkt-054.title: Conservation land trusts: private groups that protect land
nature-mkt-054.text: The Trustees of Reservations in Massachusetts, founded in 1891, was the first conservation land trust; by 2021 the US had over 1,300. Such a trust is a nonprofit that buys and looks after land, or holds conservation easements on it, to protect nature, farmland or recreation. Trusts rely on donations, grants and public programs, and landowners often donate easements or land. Many run on volunteers: in 2005, 54% of US land trusts were all-volunteer. Local and regional US trusts protected almost 9.4 million acres by 2003, double the 1998 figure.

nature-mkt-033.title: Natural Asset Companies: selling shares in nature
nature-mkt-033.text: A Natural Asset Company is a corporation set up to hold and manage natural assets so that private investors can fund conservation and land use that restores nature. Each holds rights to land or sea areas, such as forests, ranches, grasslands or marine areas, and is run to maximize their ecological value. The New York Stock Exchange proposed listing them in 2021 but withdrew in January 2024 amid political backlash. Critics on the right fear locked-up public land and speculation; critics on the left doubt markets can be trusted to look after nature.

nature-mkt-014.title: Conservation trust funds: money that lasts
nature-mkt-014.text: Short-term grants struggle to pay the running costs of a nature reserve year after year. A conservation trust fund is built for that job. It is a long-term fund that gives grants to conservation work. Many are endowments that live off their returns; others are spent down over time. Such funds help pay for managing land set aside for nature. Experience with debt-for-nature swaps helped shape them.

nature-mkt-017.title: Measuring what conservation money achieves
nature-mkt-017.text: Conservation finance deals often require reporting both how money was spent and what ecological results it achieved. Reports may separate outputs, such as area under management, from outcomes, such as changes in ecological condition. The Taskforce on Nature-related Financial Disclosures recommends reporting how a business depends on and affects nature, though gaps in data limit consistency. Payment schemes also raise questions of fairness: who can be paid, how schemes affect who holds land and how people live, and whether wealthier landholders benefit most.

nature-mkt-013.title: Where conservation money comes from
nature-mkt-013.text: Money for nature comes from three broad sources: domestic public spending, international public finance including aid, and private spending and investment. Market-rate capital can come from private investors, and from public or charitable investors working through development finance institutions and multilateral development banks. Conservation NGOs and foundations often act as go-betweens that run projects. That creates a counting problem. Because NGOs get much of their income from governments and foundations, adding up total conservation finance risks counting the same money twice. Public and charitable money is sometimes called catalytic: it covers early costs or shares risk so that private investment follows.

nature-mkt-016.title: Transaction costs: the hidden price of conservation deals
nature-mkt-016.text: Finding, assembling, checking, contracting and monitoring a conservation project all cost money. These {{ref:nature-econ-641}} are often cited as a barrier to scaling up conservation finance. They bite hardest where projects are small, varied, or need intensive monitoring and verification. They can make projects less attractive to investors and raise the cost of capital. A debt-for-nature swap, for example, needs coordination among debtor governments, creditors and NGOs.

nature-mkt-052.title: Catastrophe bonds: investors who bet against disaster
nature-mkt-052.text: Hurricane Andrew and the Northridge earthquake prompted the first catastrophe bonds in the mid-1990s. Such a bond moves a defined disaster risk from a sponsor, usually an insurer, to investors. If the named disaster happens, the principal goes to the sponsor to fund recovery; otherwise investors get it back at maturity, plus interest. Rising climate-related disaster risk has led governments and insurers to use them when reinsurance, insurance for insurers, is unavailable or too costly. Swiss Re estimated the market at $43.1 billion at the end of 2023, with a record $15.4 billion issued that year.

nature-mkt-053.title: What sets off a catastrophe bond
nature-mkt-053.text: A catastrophe bond pays out when its trigger is met. Triggers can be the insurer's actual losses, modeled losses, industry-wide losses, or measured features of the event itself. Triggers closer to the insurer's own losses protect it better; index and measured-event triggers spare investors from the insurer's claims handling. A trigger can apply to a single event or to the sum of losses over a period, usually a year. With a $90 billion threshold, for example, three $20 billion hurricanes and a $40 billion earthquake total $100 billion and trigger payout.

nature-mkt-059.title: Parametric insurance: paying out when the wind passes a line
nature-mkt-059.text: Mexico's Quintana Roo insures a coral reef with a policy triggered by wind speed, paying up to $3.8 million a year. In 2020 Hurricane Delta set off an $850,000 payout. This is parametric, or index-based, insurance: it pays a pre-set amount when a measured trigger, such as a wind speed or rainfall level, is reached. Ordinary insurance pays the assessed loss after an event. Parametric cover only checks, through weather services, sensors or satellites, that the trigger was passed. The payoff is speed and lower transaction costs. The drawback is that payouts follow the measurements, so they may not cover the full damage.

nature-mkt-018.title: Sustainable finance: seeking returns while weighing the planet
nature-mkt-018.text: Green and other sustainability-labeled bonds together reached $170 billion in 2018 and $653.5 billion in 2025. They are among the products of sustainable finance: the practices, standards, rules and products that seek financial returns while weighing environmental, social and governance concerns. The term is often used as a synonym for ESG investing. The wider field also includes {{ref:nature-mkt-030}}, {{ref:nature-mkt-060}} and ethical investing. Its reach is global. The {{ref:nature-clim-074}} asks countries to make finance flows consistent with low greenhouse gas emissions and development that can withstand climate change. Sustainable finance is also described as a cornerstone for reaching the UN's {{ref:nature-gov-010}}, adopted in 2015 with 17 goals and 169 targets. Public money stays important. Much of the money for climate goals, though, is expected to come from the private sector. Over two decades, sustainable finance grew from a niche topic into a recognized field of research and university teaching.

nature-mkt-040.title: ESG: judging companies by more than their profits
nature-mkt-040.text: By 2023, investments managed under the ESG label topped US$30 trillion. ESG, short for environmental, social and governance, is an investing approach that weighs a company's record on those three fronts alongside its finances. The term came to prominence in a 2004 UN-backed report, 'Who Cares Wins'. The environmental pillar covers issues such as emissions, biodiversity and waste, which often reflect externalities that markets do not handle. The social pillar covers effects on workers and communities. The governance pillar covers how firms are directed and controlled, including ethics, corruption and tax. A 2005 legal report for UNEP's finance initiative concluded that weighing ESG issues was permissible and arguably part of an investor's duty to clients. The backlash has been real. ESG funds saw outflows for the first time in 2023, and many US funds have dropped ESG terms from their names amid claims of misleading green marketing. Critics point to poor data and standards, and argue that big asset managers impose rules without democratic oversight. Its data, standards and political legitimacy all remain disputed.

nature-mkt-046.title: Green bonds: borrowing only for green projects
nature-mkt-046.text: The World Bank issued the first labeled green bond in 2008, a year after the European Investment Bank's Climate Awareness Bond. A green bond is a bond whose money is used only for projects with environmental benefits. Like ordinary bonds, they can be issued by governments, development banks or companies, which repay the bond plus interest. Eligible projects include renewable energy, energy efficiency, pollution control, sustainable land use, biodiversity, clean transport and adapting to climate change. Green bonds raised over $93 billion in 2016, still only around 1% of global bond issuance, and by 2024 total issuance had reached about $700 billion. Legally they barely differ from ordinary bonds: green promises are often not binding in the contract. Critics question some bonds' green credentials, as when the Climate Bonds Initiative refused to list a Repsol bond in 2017. The EU's Green Bonds Regulation, in force from 21 December 2024, created the 'European Green Bond'.

nature-mkt-030.title: Impact investing: profit with a measurable purpose
nature-mkt-030.text: Many impact investors accept expected returns 2-4 percentage points lower in exchange for measurable social impact. Impact investing puts money into companies, organizations and funds meant to produce a measurable social or environmental benefit as well as a financial return. It lines up an investor's values with where the money goes, in fields such as renewable energy, education and microfinance. It spans private equity, venture capital and debt, and targets returns from below-market to above-market. The term was coined in 2005, and modern impact funds grew prominent soon after the Great Recession. In 2024 about 3,907 organizations managed an estimated $1.571 trillion in impact assets, far smaller than the $78 trillion global stock market. The UN development goals need an estimated $5-7 trillion of investment a year, mostly expected from private capital, and impact investors linked their funds to them.

nature-mkt-019.title: Climate, green and sustainable finance: three nested terms
nature-mkt-019.text: Money for climate, green finance and sustainable finance are often treated as the same thing. The UN Environment Programme separates them as three nested circles. {{ref:nature-clim-042}}, the smallest, mainly funds adaptation, resilience, cutting emissions, and a fair shift away from fossil fuels. Green finance covers that plus other environmental issues, such as protecting biodiversity. Sustainable finance adds social and governance concerns, making it the broadest term for finance that supports development able to last. The field has a short history. One review traces three periods: forerunners from the 1970s to 2010, an early phase from 2010 to 2021, and a mature phase since 2021.

nature-mkt-020.title: Green taxonomies: official lists of what counts as green
nature-mkt-020.text: Which investments deserve the green label? A sustainable finance taxonomy answers with an official classification of the economic activities that count as green or sustainable. Its aim is to stop misleading green claims and help investors make greener choices. The European Commission set up a technical expert group in 2018 to define one, and the EU taxonomy came into force in July 2020. Investments are judged against six objectives: cutting emissions, adapting to climate change, reusing materials, pollution, water and biodiversity. The hardest calls were political. Classing fossil gas and nuclear energy as sustainable proved controversial, and some expert advisers threatened to resign over gas. Whether either belongs in the taxonomy is still disputed. The EU was not alone: Mongolia adopted a national green finance taxonomy in 2018, among the first countries to do so.

nature-mkt-042.title: Does ESG pay? The evidence on returns
nature-mkt-042.text: Milton Friedman argued that social responsibility harms a firm's financial performance. Economists still disagree about whether attention to environmental, social and governance issues raises or lowers a company's value and investors' returns. Some evidence points the other way from Friedman. A 2011 study found the '100 Best Companies to Work For' beat their peers' stock returns by 2-3% a year. Other studies link ESG indicators to higher company value. Still others warn that overinvesting in ESG can hurt it. Some research suggests an inverted U: value rises with ESG spending up to an optimal level, then falls. The results so far are mixed, from positive to negative to that middle ground, and no single answer has won out.

nature-mkt-041.title: Five ways investors put their values to work
nature-mkt-041.text: The best-known early case of responsible investing was the disinvestment from South Africa in the 1970s and 1980s, in protest against apartheid. Today responsible investors steer money using five main methods. Positive selection picks companies that meet ESG criteria, or the best performers in each sector. Exclusion removes sectors or firms from consideration on ESG grounds. Integration adds ESG risks and opportunities to ordinary financial analysis. Engagement and activism use dialogue with companies and shareholder voting to push them to change. Each method has trade-offs. Screening, for example, brings its own risks, such as concentrating money in a few sectors.

nature-mkt-077.title: Eco-investing: betting on clean technology
nature-mkt-077.text: One tracker estimated that over $1.248 trillion has been invested in solar, wind, geothermal, ocean and other green sectors since 2007. Eco-investing, or green investing, is investing by values focused on companies that offer environmentally friendly products and practices. Unlike the broader field, it narrows to environmental issues, especially renewable energy and clean technology. New green technologies carry high up-front costs, which are harder to justify to investors.

nature-mkt-023.title: Aggregate confusion: why ESG scores disagree
nature-mkt-023.text: Credit ratings from the largest agencies agree 99% of the time. One paper found that ESG ratings agree only 60% of the time. This spread is called the ESG ratings gap, or 'aggregate confusion'. Sustainable finance lacks a single accepted standard for measuring and reporting sustainability, so companies and funds are hard to compare. Many bodies write standards independently, including the GRI, the IFRS Foundation and the Carbon Disclosure Project, which has confused companies and investors. Because standards vary and change, some funds labeled ESG still hold oil and coal shares.

nature-mkt-022.title: Green central banking: should central banks fight climate change?
nature-mkt-022.text: In 2018 eight central banks created the Network for Greening the Financial System, which has grown to nearly 116 central banks and supervisors. Green central banking is the idea that central banks should use their powers to help cut emissions and steer money to green investment. Their tools include {{ref:nature-econ-560}} and rules on how much capital banks hold. Banks have proposed lighter capital rules for green loans, while central bankers and nonprofits prefer heavier charges on fossil-fuel assets. Many researchers argue that such goals strain the legitimacy of independent central banks, whose mandates rarely include climate aims, and the question remains disputed.

nature-mkt-021.title: Disclosure rules: making companies report climate risk
nature-mkt-021.text: In 2015 the Financial Stability Board launched a climate disclosure taskforce. Its job was to push firms to report the risks climate change poses them and how they govern those risks. Sustainability disclosure rules ask companies to report climate and other sustainability risks and impacts so investors can judge them. Voluntary rules have limited effect, research shows. An EU reporting directive adopted in October 2022 makes reporting compulsory for more firms, widening coverage from about 11,700 companies to about 50,000.

nature-mkt-062.title: Sustainability bonds: green and social at once
nature-mkt-062.text: Green, social and sustainability bonds differ in which projects their money may fund. A sustainability bond must fund a mix of both green and social projects. The ICMA principles, from the International Capital Market Association, are the most widely accepted framework for issuing all three kinds. Critics still warn of misleading claims, because no single definition says what makes a bond sustainable.

nature-mkt-043.title: ESG rating agencies: the scorekeepers of responsible investing
nature-mkt-043.text: Sustainalytics counted over 600 ESG-rating companies in 2018, though takeovers are concentrating the market. These agencies score companies on their environmental, social and governance performance and are the main source of information for ESG investing. Each uses its own metrics, and no industry-wide standard exists. Scores can mislead the unwary. Risk raters measure how exposed a firm is to ESG risks, so a high score need not mean a strong positive effect on the world.

nature-mkt-044.title: The Equator Principles: banks' rules for risky projects
nature-mkt-044.text: By October 2019, 97 institutions in 37 countries had adopted the Equator Principles, covering most international project finance debt. Launched in 2003 and based on International Finance Corporation policies, the principles are a framework banks use to assess and manage environmental and social risk in project finance. Adopting banks commit not to lend to projects whose borrowers cannot meet their social and environmental policies.

nature-mkt-045.title: The Principles for Responsible Investment
nature-mkt-045.text: Set up in 2005, the Principles for Responsible Investment are a UN-backed framework for investors. They help investors analyze environmental, social and governance issues and act as responsible owners of the companies they hold. As of April 2019 the framework had over 2,350 signatories.

nature-mkt-048.title: The greenium: paying extra to be green
nature-mkt-048.text: Investors want green bonds badly enough to accept less for them. The greenium is the lower yield, or pricing premium, that green bonds often carry because of that demand. Studies find high demand gives green bonds lower yields than ordinary equivalents. Estimates vary widely: from -85 to +213 basis points when bonds are first sold, and -1 to -9 basis points on average when they are traded later. A basis point is one hundredth of a percentage point. Voluntary labels with weak oversight leave room for false green claims, which may lead investors to accept lower returns than on ordinary, or brown, investments.

nature-mkt-072.title: Fiduciary duty and ESG: may investors weigh the planet?
nature-mkt-072.text: A 2015 report, 'Fiduciary Duty in the 21st Century', concluded that ignoring long-term value drivers, ESG among them, is itself a failure of fiduciary duty. A 2005 legal report for UNEP had found that weighing ESG issues was permissible and arguably required. In the United States, some question whether pension funds that weigh such factors break their duty to maximize returns. One state pension board blocked selling off its fossil fuel holdings on those grounds, though a 2019 analysis found the divested fund would have earned more. Investors and lawyers still dispute whether this legal duty bars ESG.

nature-mkt-032.title: Environmental investing: impact investing for the planet
nature-mkt-032.text: By 2024 green bonds had reached about $700 billion of total issuance, and all sustainability-related bonds nearly $8 trillion. Environmental investing is the branch of impact investing aimed at a measurable positive effect on the environment alongside financial returns. It funds projects such as clean energy, public transport and sustainable water management. It arose from the recognition that tackling climate change needs huge private sums.

nature-mkt-031.title: Mission investing: foundations putting endowments to work
nature-mkt-031.text: A foundation's endowment can do more than fund grants. Mission investments are investments by foundations, from part or all of their endowment, that further their charitable goals while earning a return. Program-related investments are made mainly for charitable aims at below-market terms, such as recoverable grants and cheap loans. For US private foundations they count toward the required 5 percent annual payout. Mission-related investments seek market-rate returns from mission-driven organizations while helping the endowment grow.

nature-mkt-060.title: Social finance: private money for public needs
nature-mkt-060.text: Social finance grew quickly after the 2008 financial crisis, as investors sought ethical alternatives. It is financial services that use private capital to tackle social and environmental needs while giving investors a return. Unlike philanthropy, it sustains itself by being profitable rather than relying on donors. It has no agreed definition, but includes impact investing, investing by values and lending to social enterprises. It struggles with low returns, high start-up and regulatory costs, neglect by mainstream banks and poor access to ordinary savers. Critics argue it pulls money from productive uses, while backers say it adds investment where charity is declining.

nature-mkt-061.title: Social impact bonds: investors paid only for success
nature-mkt-061.text: The first social impact bond, launched in the UK in 2010, funded the rehabilitation of prisoners at Peterborough Prison. In such a contract, private investors fund a public program, and the government repays them only if agreed goals are met. Unlike ordinary bonds, they have no fixed return. By 2022 there were 276 projects with $745m raised, used in 23 countries as of May 2023. Backers say taxpayers pay only for success; critics say the bonds displace other funding and are an expensive way to run programs.

nature-mkt-063.title: Sustainability-linked bonds: interest tied to targets
nature-mkt-063.text: In September 2019 the Italian utility Enel issued the first sustainability-linked bond, promising a 25 basis point penalty on its interest if it missed its target. The terms of such a bond, such as its interest rate, change depending on whether the issuer meets set sustainability targets, tracked with key performance indicators. Unlike green, social or sustainability bonds, the money raised can be used for any purpose. Issuance was around $5 billion in 2019 and $10.6 billion in 2020. Over 85% were tied to environmental measures, most often cutting emissions.

nature-mkt-080.title: Blue bonds: green bonds for the ocean
nature-mkt-080.text: A blue bond is the ocean version of a green bond. It raises money specifically for ocean conservation and sustainable activity at sea. Like green bonds, blue bonds earmark money for eligible projects and usually follow voluntary guidance on use of proceeds, project selection, management and reporting. Bonds tied to sustainable fisheries, such as the Seychelles government's blue bond, are discussed as a way to bring private capital to nature.

nature-mkt-047.title: The Green Bond Principles
nature-mkt-047.text: The Green Bond Principles are voluntary guidance from the International Capital Market Association on how green bonds should be run. They recommend a defined use of the money raised, a process for choosing projects, careful management of the funds and regular reporting, sometimes with outside review. These practices aim to narrow the information gap between issuers and investors and to support accountability.

reviews.finance-for-conservation: This chapter laid out the tools of finance, from bonds and shares to return on investment and diversification, and then followed them into conservation. Older routes such as foreign aid, debt-for-nature swaps and land trusts still matter, but the gap between needs and actual flows has pushed the field toward private capital. Blended finance, green and blue bonds, impact investing and catastrophe bonds all try to make protecting nature pay investors a return. The same questions follow every tool: whether results are additional and lasting, whether labels are honest, and whether ESG scores that agree only 60% of the time can guide anyone. Behind it all sits a plain economic fact: activities that harm biodiversity usually earn profits, while conservation must find its money.
